summary: Messaging Layer Security (MLS, RFC 9420) lets a group of people share encryption keys for private messaging. This informational RFC describes the architecture for using MLS in a messaging service, including the roles of the pieces involved, and the security properties and limits that follow from that design.

eli5.summary: A group chat needs one secret that only members know, even as people join and leave. This explains how the pieces of a secure group chat system fit together and what protection you get.

how do new members join an mls group
subtitle: How secure group messaging systems work

tldr.problem: Large group chats need a shared secret that only members know, and that secret must change as people join and leave, all without central servers being able to decrypt messages.
tldr.mechanism: MLS defines two services (an Authentication Service to verify who people are, and a Delivery Service to route messages) and a protocol where group members form a tree structure, with members rotating encryption keys through a ratcheting mechanism. New members join via Welcome messages encrypted with their public keys.
tldr.outcome: Applications can build secure group messaging that protects messages even if the central server is compromised, and provides forward secrecy so old messages stay secret even if a device is hacked later.

today: RFC 9750 is an informational RFC that describes the architecture for MLS as a reference for implementers and system designers. The actual MLS protocol specification is in RFC 9420. This architecture document remains the authoritative guide for how to build messaging systems using MLS.

sections.title: Introduction to MLS
sections.content:
Messaging Layer Security (MLS) solves a problem for group messaging: how to keep messages secret from the server operator, even as people join and leave the group. The protocol is not a complete messaging application but rather a cryptographic layer that sits under applications like Signal or WhatsApp could use.

MLS works with two key services: an Authentication Service that confirms who people are, and a Delivery Service that routes messages around. The clever part is that even if the Delivery Service is compromised, it cannot read the group messages or forge them. Clients do the real encryption.
sections.eli5: MLS is like a locked box inside a UPS truck. The truck (Delivery Service) cannot open the box, and the security guard (Authentication Service) just confirms you are who you say you are.

sections.title: Architecture: Services and Roles
sections.content:
MLS architecture has two abstract services. The Authentication Service (AS) certifies that a public key belongs to a particular person and can verify credentials. It does not need to be a single server; it could be a PKI (Public Key Infrastructure), a Key Transparency log, or manual key fingerprint verification.

The Delivery Service (DS) receives and forwards messages. It stores initial keying material (called KeyPackages) that new members need to join a group. The DS acts like a broadcaster: a sender sends one message, and the DS copies it to all group members. Importantly, the DS does not need to be trustworthy for security; even a hostile DS cannot decrypt messages or impersonate members.

MLS specifies a Proposal-Commit pattern for group changes. A Proposal announces a change (add a user, remove a user, rotate keys). A Commit applies proposals and moves the group to a new cryptographic epoch. This two-step process ensures all members agree on the new state.
sections.eli5: The Authentication Service is like an ID checker at the door. The Delivery Service is like a mailroom that copies your letter to everyone. Two-step changes (Proposal then Commit) are like suggesting a rule and then voting to enforce it.

sections.title: How Groups Form and Operate
sections.content:
When Alice wants to create a group with Bob, she first gets Bob's initial keying material from the DS. She then sends two messages: a Commit message to the group announcing that Bob is joining, and a Welcome message encrypted just for Bob with the group's secret. Bob decrypts the Welcome message (which only he can read, because it uses his public encryption key), and now he and Alice share the group secret.

Every time someone joins or leaves, the group secret changes. This is called advancing to a new epoch. Each epoch has its own shared secret, so if Bob leaves, he cannot read any messages sent after his departure.

Within a group, the members are stored as leaves of a binary tree. This tree structure lets the protocol encrypt to subsets efficiently and helps manage the group state. Members update their positions in the tree as the group changes.

The protocol supports both internal joins (where an existing member adds a new member) and external joins (where a new member joins by publishing a GroupInfo object that anyone with access to it can use to join).
sections.eli5: Alice hands Bob a secret envelope (Welcome message). Bob opens it and gets the group secret. When Charlie joins, everyone makes a new secret so Charlie starts fresh. The group is like a tree where each person is a leaf.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
MLS provides three core security guarantees. Message Confidentiality means only group members can read messages; Message Authentication means you know who sent a message and it was not tampered with; and Message Integrity means you can detect if a message was modified.

Forward Secrecy (FS) means that if an attacker steals all of Alice's keys today, old messages sent before this epoch stay secret. This works because old encryption keys are deleted after use. Post-Compromise Security (PCS) means that if Alice's device is compromised at time t1 but she updates her keys at time t2, all messages after t2 are protected again, even though the attacker saw everything up to t2.

MLS assumes the Internet threat model: attackers can read all network traffic and inject or delete messages. It does not depend on the transport being secure (like TLS), though using a secure transport is recommended to protect metadata. The protocol protects application data even if the Delivery Service is compromised, but not all metadata such as group membership.

The protocol does not protect against all attacks. It provides no protection against replay by insiders (a member cannot be prevented from replaying old messages they received). It also does not guarantee that all members process the same commit in the same order if the network is partitioned.
sections.eli5: Old messages stay secret even if your phone is stolen today. If you update your keys, future messages are safe again. But if your friend is an attacker, they can share old messages you sent to them.

sections.title: Building a System with MLS
sections.content:
An application using MLS must make many decisions. It must choose an Authentication Service and decide how credentials are verified. It must decide whether group operation messages (Proposals and Commits) are encrypted or in plaintext; plaintext is faster but leaks group structure to the server.

The application must handle message ordering. Some designs use strongly consistent systems (like an "ordering server" that all clients trust to order messages the same way); others use eventually consistent systems where clients handle reordering themselves. The Delivery Service can help with ordering, but a malicious DS can reorder messages or partition the group.

Applications must define policies: which members can add others, how long members can stay idle, how to rotate keys, whether external joins are allowed, and what cipher suites are in use. All clients must follow the same policies or they will disagree about what is valid.

The RFC recommends ensuring KeyPackages are rotated frequently, using strong transport encryption, and having clients detect and remove idle members. It also recommends credential validation be uniform across the group so all clients reject the same invalid credentials.
sections.eli5: You have to decide: Is the mailroom trusted to order letters? Can anyone invite new members, or only admins? How often should everyone refresh their keys?
